title: One percent loss that ruins everything
tagline: Ping looks perfect. Video calls stutter, file copies crawl, and the switch reports no errors. The link is running at half duplex.
environment: Fedora file server with a 1 Gbps NIC
Video conferencing and large file transfers
No monitoring on interface error counters
topology: clients --[access switch, Gi0/12]--> server eth0 (1 Gbps)
symptoms: ping shows 0% loss and 0.3 ms RTT
Video calls stutter and drop; large transfers run at 2-5 MB/s instead of 100 MB/s
The switch reports no CRC errors and no discards
The problem started after a switch port was replaced
objectives: Explain why small-packet tests can look perfect while throughput collapses
Read duplex and collision counters as evidence rather than as trivia
Distinguish a duplex mismatch from genuine packet loss and from an MTU problem
framework: Is the loss size-dependent, rate-dependent, or constant?
What do the interface counters say at both ends?
Do both ends agree on speed and duplex?

evidence.label: The misleading baseline
evidence.output:
20 packets transmitted, 20 received, 0% packet loss, time 19020ms
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 0.241/0.302/0.412/0.041 ms
evidence.insight: Small, infrequent packets are almost never affected by a duplex mismatch. A clean ping is not evidence that the link is healthy.

evidence.label: Throughput reality
evidence.output:
[ ID] Interval           Transfer     Bitrate         Retr
[  5]   0.00-5.00   sec  11.2 MBytes  18.8 Mbits/sec  412
[  5]   0.00-5.00   sec   sender
[  5]   0.00-5.00   sec   receiver
evidence.insight: 18.8 Mbit/s on a 1 Gbps link with 412 retransmissions. Throughput is roughly 2% of capacity, which is the classic signature of a duplex mismatch: collisions destroy most large frames.

evidence.label: What the NIC thinks the link is
evidence.output:
Speed: 1000Mb/s
	Duplex: Half
	Link detected: yes
evidence.insight: The server's NIC negotiated half duplex. A 1 Gbps link cannot legitimately be half duplex — 1000BASE-T is always full duplex — so this is a forced/auto-negotiation mismatch, not a real capability.

evidence.label: Error counters on the server
evidence.output:
2: eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc fq_codel state UP mode DEFAULT
    RX:  bytes packets errors dropped  missed   mcast
   918223311  812334   0       0       0        12
    TX:  bytes packets errors dropped carrier collsns
  1122334455  998211   0       0       0     18842
evidence.insight: 18,842 transmit collisions and zero receive errors. Collisions on a full-duplex-capable link mean the two ends disagree about duplex: the half-duplex side senses the other side's simultaneous transmission as a collision.

evidence.label: What the switch port says
evidence.output:
Full-duplex, 1000Mb/s, media type is 10/100/1000BaseTX
  0 input errors, 0 CRC, 0 frame, 0 overrun, 0 ignored
  0 output errors, 0 collisions, 0 interface resets
  18842 late collision
evidence.insight: The switch is full duplex and sees late collisions. Late collisions are the fingerprint: the switch transmitted while the server was also transmitting, which only happens when one side is half duplex.

evidence.label: TCP-level confirmation
evidence.output:
cubic wscale:7,7 rto:204 rtt:0.31/0.12 ato:40 mss:1448 pmtu:1500 rcvmss:1448
	 retrans:0/412 bytes_retrans:611234 segs_out:8122 segs_in:4411
	 send 18.8Mbps pacing_rate 37.6Mbps delivery_rate 4.1Mbps
evidence.insight: 412 retransmissions with a tiny RTT. Low latency plus heavy retransmission is not congestion — congestion would show a rising RTT. It is loss caused by the link itself.

hypotheses.why: RTT is 0.31 ms and the link is at 2% utilisation; congestion would raise latency and queueing, not produce collisions.

hypotheses.text: The server NIC is running half duplex while the switch is full duplex, so collisions destroy large frames.
hypotheses.why: ethtool reports half duplex at 1000 Mb/s, the server counts 18,842 TX collisions, and the switch reports late collisions.

hypotheses.text: The MTU is wrong on the path.
hypotheses.why: An MTU problem produces size-dependent failure with no ACKs for large segments, not collisions and retransmissions at low RTT.
A bad cable produces CRC and input errors; both ends report zero CRC and zero input errors.

solution.root_cause: The switch port was configured with a fixed speed/duplex while the server NIC uses autonegotiation. Autonegotiation failed to agree, so the server fell back to half duplex at 1000 Mb/s while the switch stayed full duplex. The half-duplex side treats the switch's simultaneous transmissions as collisions, and every collision destroys a large frame, so throughput collapses while small pings still succeed.
solution.resolution: Set both ends to autonegotiate (the correct default for 1000BASE-T), or if a fixed setting is genuinely required, fix both ends identically. On the server: ethtool -s eth0 autoneg on (and remove any forced speed/duplex from NetworkManager or the interface configuration so it survives a reboot). On the switch: no speed nonegotiate / speed auto / duplex auto on Gi0/12.
solution.verification: ethtool reports Speed 1000Mb/s, Duplex Full, and 'Link partner advertised ... Full'; ip -s link shows collisions no longer incrementing; iperf3 reaches hundreds of Mbit/s with near-zero retransmissions; ss -ti shows retrans:0; and the switch's late-collision counter stops rising.
lessons: A clean ping proves reachability, not health. It uses tiny packets at a low rate.
Collisions on a modern switched link mean a duplex disagreement, not normal operation.
Late collisions are the fingerprint of one side being half duplex. Read counters at both ends.
interview_followups: What is the difference between an early collision and a late collision?
Why is forcing speed and duplex considered bad practice?

resolution_options.why: The standard and correct configuration for 1000BASE-T; both ends then agree on full duplex.
Also works, but only if both ends are changed together and documented; autonegotiation is preferred.
No CRC or input errors, so the physical medium is not the problem.
The bottleneck is frame loss from collisions, not the window.

resolution_options.text: Add a second NIC and bond them
resolution_options.why: Adds cost and complexity while leaving the duplex mismatch in place on both links.

interview_questions.q: Ping is clean but throughput is terrible. What are the candidates?
interview_questions.a: Duplex mismatch, MTU/PMTUD black hole, a rate limit or policer, a saturated or erroring link, or an application-level bottleneck. The distinguishing evidence is counters (collisions vs CRC), a size sweep (MTU), and RTT behaviour (congestion).

A station transmitting after the slot time has passed, which on a switched link almost always means one side is half duplex and did not defer to the other's transmission. It is the signature of a duplex mismatch.

interview_questions.q: Why should speed and duplex be left on auto?
interview_questions.a: Autonegotiation is the only way both ends agree on capabilities, and 1000BASE-T requires it. Forcing one side disables negotiation and commonly produces a duplex mismatch, which is worse than the problem it was meant to solve.
